title: How to Scrape Kalshi with Python: Markets, Order Books, Price History, and a Snapshot Tracker (2026)
author: Viktor
summary: Kalshi has become one of the more interesting public datasets around. Every market is a running, money-backed estimate of how likely something is: an election, a Fed decision, tomorrow's high temperature in New York. If you do research, build dashboards, or want to compare Kalshi against polls or other prediction markets, you'll want that data in your own database. The good news is that you don't need to scrape HTML at all. The Kalshi API serves market data publicly, with no key and no login. The less good news is that it has a handful of quirks that will quietly give you wrong numbers if you don't know about them. In this post I'll build a small Python Kalshi scraper that: Pages through every open market in a series Reads the order book the right way (it only lists bids, more on that below) Exports hourly price candles to CSV Stores a snapshot on every run in SQLite, so you can see which markets moved Everything here was run against the live API in October 2026. Before you start: read Kalshi's API docs and Terms of Service, keep request rates low, and don't redistribute the data commercially without checking what you're allowed to do. This tutorial only reads public market data. It doesn't place orders and doesn't need an account. Your options, briefly Public market data endpoints (this post). GET requests under https://api.elections.kalshi.com/trade-api/v2 for markets, events, series, order books, trades, and candlesticks. No auth needed. Authenticated API. You need an account and an RSA-signed API key for anything that touches your portfolio: orders, fills, balance, and a few account endpoints. You don't need it for reading markets. WebSocket feed. Better if you want real-time ticks, but it needs an authenticated connection and you have to handle reconnects yourself. For a snapshot every few minutes, REST is simpler. Scraping kalshi.com HTML. Don't bother. The site is a JavaScript app that calls the same API anyway. How Kalshi data is shaped There are three levels, and the tickers tell you where you are: Series KXHIGHNY "Highest temperature in NYC" (recurring) Event KXHIGHNY-26OCT21 one occurrence: Oct 21, 2026 Market KXHIGHNY-26OCT21-T66 one yes/no contract: "above 66°?" A market is always a binary yes/no contract that pays $1. Prices are in dollars between 0 and 1, so a YES price of 0.23 means the market puts it at roughly 23%. To get a series ticker from a market page, look at the URL. On kalshi.com/markets/kxhighny/... , the first path segment uppercased ( KXHIGHNY ) is the series ticker. Step 1: A polite request helper Install the one dependency: pip install requests The Kalshi docs say a rate-limited request returns 429 with {"error": "too many requests"} , no Retry-After header , and no penalty. So you just back off and try again. Authenticated Basic-tier accounts get a read budget of about 20 requests per second. I couldn't find a documented number for anonymous calls, so I stay far below that. import csv import sqlite3 import sys import time from datetime import datetime , timezone from decimal import Decimal import requests BASE = " https://api.elections.kalshi.com/trade-api/v2 " session = requests . Session () session . headers . update ({ " User-Agent " : " kalshi-scraper-tutorial/1.0 (you@example.com) " }) def get ( path , params = None , max_retries = 5 ): """ GET with backoff on 429 and 5xx. """ for attempt in range ( max_retries ): res = session . get ( f " { BASE }{ path } " , params = params , timeout = 20 ) if res . status_code == 429 or res . status_code >= 500 : wait = 2 ** attempt print ( f " { res . status_code } on { path } , sleeping { wait } s " , file = sys . stderr ) time . sleep ( wait ) continue res . raise_for_status () return res . json () raise RuntimeError ( f " gave up on { path } after { max_retries } tries " ) Setting a descriptive User-Agent with a contact address costs nothing and makes it easier for the other side if your script ever misbehaves. Step 2: The core of the Kalshi scraper, paging markets with a cursor GET /markets takes series_ticker , event_ticker , status , limit (I use 200), and cursor . Each response includes a cursor . When it's empty, you're done. def iter_markets ( series_ticker , status = " open " , page_size = 200 ): cursor = None while True : params = { " series_ticker " : series_ticker , " status " : status , " limit " : page_size } if cursor : params [ " cursor " ] = cursor data = get ( " /markets " , params ) yield from data . get ( " markets " , []) cursor = data . get ( " cursor " ) if not cursor : break time . sleep ( 0.25 ) # be polite Two things surprised me here. The status you filter by isn't the status you get back. You ask for status=open , but the records come back with "status": "active" . If you filter again on your side with == "open" , you'll get zero rows and spend ten minutes thinking pagination is broken. Unfiltered listings are full of combo markets. If you call /markets?status=open without a series or event, the first pages are auto-generated multi-leg "combo" markets with tickers like KXMVECROSSCATEGORY-... , mostly with zero volume. Add mve_filter=exclude to leave them out, or better, always scope by series_ticker or event_ticker . Step 3: Turn markets into clean rows Here's the part that bites people who copy older tutorials: Kalshi sends prices and sizes as strings , with suffixes on the field names. Older posts use integer-cent fields like yes_bid and volume . What you get now looks like this: "yes_bid_dollars" : "0.0100" , "yes_ask_dollars" : "0.0200" , "last_price_dollars" : "0.0200" , "volume_fp" : "2428.47" , "open_interest_fp" : "2252.09" _dollars is a price, _fp is a fixed-point count (contracts can be fractional now). I parse them as Decimal so I never get 0.30000000000000004 in a report: def d ( value ): """ Kalshi sends prices and sizes as strings. Keep them exact. """ return Decimal ( value ) if value not in ( None , "" ) else None def to_row ( m ): return { " ticker " : m [ " ticker " ], " event_ticker " : m [ " event_ticker " ], " title " : m . get ( " title " ), " subtitle " : m . get ( " yes_sub_title " ), " status " : m . get ( " status " ), " close_time " : m . get ( " close_time " ), " yes_bid " : d ( m . get ( " yes_bid_dollars " )), " yes_ask " : d ( m . get ( " yes_ask_dollars " )), " last_price " : d ( m . get ( " last_price_dollars " )), " volume " : d ( m . get ( " volume_fp " )), " volume_24h " : d ( m . get ( " volume_24h_fp " )), " open_interest " : d ( m . get ( " open_interest_fp " )), } If you read a field that doesn't exist anymore, .get() just returns None . So when your dashboard shows empty columns after a Kalshi update, check the field names first. Step 4: Read the order book the right way GET /markets/{ticker}/orderbook returns this: { "orderbook_fp" : { "no_dollars" : [[ "0.9600" , "441.00" ],[ "0.9700" , "592.00" ],[ "0.9800" , "398.00" ]], "yes_dollars" : [[ "0.0100" , "286.82" ]] }} Notice that there are no asks. Kalshi only lists bids for YES and bids for NO. Because a YES and a NO together always pay $1, a NO bid at 0.98 works the same as a YES ask at 0.02. So the best YES ask is 1 - best NO bid : def best_levels ( ticker ): ob = get ( f " /markets/ { ticker } /orderbook " , { " depth " : 5 })[ " orderbook_fp " ] yes_bids = ob . get ( " yes_dollars " ) or [] no_bids = ob . get ( " no_dollars " ) or [] best_yes_bid = max (( Decimal ( p ) for p , _ in yes_bids ), default = None ) best_no_bid = max (( Decimal ( p ) for p , _ in no_bids ), default = None ) # Only bids are listed. A NO bid at 0.97 is a YES ask at 0.03. implied_yes_ask = ( Decimal ( " 1 " ) - best_no_bid ) if best_no_bid is not None else None return best_yes_bid , implied_yes_ask Levels are sorted with the best price last, which is why I use max() instead of trusting the order. An empty side comes back as missing or empty, so handle None . In my run, one of the busiest markets had no YES bids at all, because it was all but settled at zero. Step 5: Snapshots in SQLite The market list only tells you the current state. To see what moved, store a snapshot on every run: SCHEMA = """ CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS snapshots ( taken_at TEXT NOT NULL, ticker TEXT NOT NULL, event_ticker TEXT, title TEXT, yes_bid TEXT, yes_ask TEXT, last_price TEXT, volume TEXT, open_interest TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (taken_at, ticker) ); """ def snapshot ( series_ticker , db_path = " kalshi.db " ): taken_at = datetime . now ( timezone . utc ). replace ( microsecond = 0 ). isoformat () rows = [ to_row ( m ) for m in iter_markets ( series_ticker )] con = sqlite3 . connect ( db_path ) con . executescript ( SCHEMA ) con . executemany ( """ INSERT OR IGNORE INTO snapshots VALUES (:taken_at, :ticker, :event_ticker, :title, :yes_bid, :yes_ask, :last_price, :volume, :open_interest) """ , [{ ** r , ** { k : str ( r [ k ]) if r [ k ] is not None else None for k in ( " yes_bid " , " yes_ask " , " last_price " , " volume " , " open_interest " )}, " taken_at " : taken_at } for r in rows ], ) con . commit () con . close () return rows I store numbers as text so the Decimal values round-trip exactly. Cast them when you query. Here's "which markets moved the most since the last run": WITH ranked AS ( SELECT ticker , title , taken_at , CAST ( last_price AS REAL ) AS price , ROW_NUMBER () OVER ( PARTITION BY ticker ORDER BY taken_at DESC ) AS rn FROM snapshots ) SELECT a . ticker , b . price AS before , a . price AS now , ROUND ( a . price - b . price , 4 ) AS move FROM ranked a JOIN ranked b ON a . ticker = b . ticker AND b . rn = 2 WHERE a . rn = 1 ORDER BY ABS ( a . price - b . price ) DESC LIMIT 10 ; Run it from cron every 15 minutes and you have a basic movers report. Step 6: Hourly price history to CSV For history you don't need your own snapshots. The candlesticks endpoint needs the series ticker in the path as well as the market ticker. That's easy to miss: def candles ( series_ticker , ticker , hours = 48 , interval = 60 ): end = int ( time . time ()) start = end - hours * 3600 data = get ( f " /series/ { series_ticker } /markets/ { ticker } /candlesticks " , { " start_ts " : start , " end_ts " : end , " period_interval " : interval }, ) out = [] for c in data . get ( " candlesticks " , []): price = c . get ( " price " , {}) out . append ({ " end " : datetime . fromtimestamp ( c [ " end_period_ts " ], timezone . utc ). isoformat (), " close " : price . get ( " close_dollars " ), # None when nothing traded " yes_bid_close " : c . get ( " yes_bid " , {}). get ( " close_dollars " ), " yes_ask_close " : c . get ( " yes_ask " , {}). get ( " close_dollars " ), " volume " : c . get ( " volume_fp " ), " open_interest " : c . get ( " open_interest_fp " ), }) return out period_interval is in minutes and accepts 1 , 60 , or 1440 . Each candle has price (trades), yes_bid and yes_ask (quotes), plus volume and open interest. In hours with no trades, the price values can come back empty. Don't fill those gaps with zeros, or your chart will show a crash that never happened. Putting the Kalshi scraper together if __name__ == " __main__ " : series = sys . argv [ 1 ] if len ( sys . argv ) > 1 else " KXHIGHNY " rows = snapshot ( series ) rows . sort ( key = lambda r : r [ " volume_24h " ] or 0 , reverse = True ) print ( f " { len ( rows ) } open markets in { series } " ) for r in rows [: 5 ]: print ( f ' { r [ " ticker " ] : < 28 } bid { r [ " yes_bid " ] } ask { r [ " yes_ask " ] } 24h vol { r [ " volume_24h " ] } { r [ " subtitle " ] } ' ) if rows : top = rows [ 0 ][ " ticker " ] bid , ask = best_levels ( top ) print ( f " \n Order book for { top } : best YES bid { bid } , implied YES ask { ask } " ) history = candles ( series , top ) with open ( f " { top } .csv " , " w " , newline = "" ) as f : w = csv . DictWriter ( f , fieldnames = history [ 0 ]. keys () if history else [ " end " ]) w . writeheader () w . writerows ( history ) print ( f " wrote { len ( history ) } hourly candles to { top } .csv " ) Real output from a run on the NYC temperature series: 12 open markets in KXHIGHNY KXHIGHNY-26OCT20-B69.5 bid 0.0000 ask 0.0100 24h vol 63785.26 69° to 70° KXHIGHNY-26OCT20-B71.5 bid 0.0000 ask 0.0100 24h vol 45825.52 71° to 72° KXHIGHNY-26OCT20-B65.5 bid 0.0000 ask 0.0100 24h vol 33171.92 65° to 66° KXHIGHNY-26OCT20-B67.5 bid 0.9900 ask 1.0000 24h vol 27363.99 67° to 68° Order book for KXHIGHNY-26OCT20-B69.5: best YES bid None, implied YES ask 0.0100 wrote 38 hourly candles to KXHIGHNY-26OCT20-B69.5.csv One more quirk shows up in that output. Yesterday's markets are still in the open list, priced at 0.01 or 0.99, because trading has stopped but they haven't been settled yet. If you're looking for live opinion, filter on close_time in the future, or you'll be ranking markets that are already decided. The walls you'll hit Schema drift. The move from integer cents to _dollars and _fp strings broke many older scripts without any error message. Log a warning when an expected field is missing instead of quietly writing None . Rate limits without hints. A 429 doesn't tell you how long to wait. Use exponential backoff and a small sleep between pages. If you're polling hundreds of order books, you'll hit the limit faster than you expect. Volume and pagination. Some series, like sports and crypto, have thousands of markets. Scope by series or event and limit columns to what you need. Settled vs. closed vs. active. Status values in filters and records don't match one to one. Write down which states you care about and test them. What isn't in the public API. Trader profiles, the leaderboard, and comments are on the website but not in the public market data endpoints. Scraping those means dealing with the web app itself, which is much more fragile. Terms. Market data is public, but that doesn't make every use OK. Read Kalshi's terms before you publish or resell anything. When DIY stops being worth it For a few series checked every 15 minutes, the script above is all you need, and it's free. It gets tedious when you track a lot of series, want Polymarket and Kalshi in the same format, or need the profile and leaderboard data that the public market endpoints don't have. At that point I'd use a hosted API. I use ScrapeAtlas* for this. Its /v1/kalshi/markets endpoint takes series , event , tickers , status , closesAfter / closesBefore , cursor , and limit (1 to 200). It leaves out combo markets by default ( combos=include brings them back) and returns the same _dollars / _fp field names you saw above, plus a nextCursor : import os import requests def api_markets ( series , cursor = None ): params = { " series " : series , " status " : " open " , " limit " : 200 } if cursor : params [ " cursor " ] = cursor res = requests . get ( " https://api.scrapeatlas.com/v1/kalshi/markets " , params = params , headers = { " x-api-key " : os . environ [ " SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY " ]}, timeout = 30 , ) res . raise_for_status () data = res . json () # data["status"]: "success" or "partial"; data["coverage"]["warnings"] explains gaps return data . get ( " markets " , []), data . get ( " nextCursor " ) Because the field names match, to_row() works unchanged. There are also /v1/kalshi/price-history , /v1/kalshi/orderbook , /v1/kalshi/trades , /v1/kalshi/leaderboard , and /v1/kalshi/profile endpoints if you need history, depth, or trader data. Wrapping up Use the public API, not HTML. Kalshi market data is a GET request away, with no key. Parse _dollars and _fp strings as Decimal , and don't trust tutorials that use integer-cent fields. The order book only has bids. YES ask = 1 − best NO bid. Scope by series or event , exclude combos, and filter out markets that are closed but not yet settled. Snapshot on a schedule if you care about movement. Use candlesticks if you only need history. If something in the API changes and the script breaks, leave a comment and I'll update the post. *I build it.

title: I built myself a morning radio station (audience: one)
author: AMiN
summary: At 7am, my phone buzzes. There’s a tall dashboard image in WhatsApp, followed by a voice note. The image shows my top tasks, job pipeline and project status. The voice talks me through the same board, starting with a fresh “G’day”. It’s a tiny radio station that broadcasts to an audience of one. I built it for myself, in spare hours, and on 17 October 2026 I open-sourced it as Chucka, also known as MorningDashboard. Why Chucka? In Australia, Chucka is a name shared by several distinct, well-known cockatoos. I liked the distinctly Aussie connection and the cheeky personality it brings to the project. Cockatoos certainly know how to make themselves heard, and my little automation does something similar: it pipes up every morning with a fresh greeting and a rundown of the day ahead. It describes what it does; Chucka gives it a noisy character of its own. You want to see the real one? The idea was simple: I already had the information I needed in Obsidian. I didn’t need another app to check. I wanted that information to find me. A picture and a voice note Every morning at 07:00 AM, Chucka sends two things to my own WhatsApp. First is a dashboard image. Python and Pillow render it directly from the live files in my Obsidian vault. It brings together the day’s top must-dos, my job pipeline and the current state of my projects. Second is a WhatsApp voice-note bubble, roughly 170 words and about 60–70 seconds long. It summarises the same board, with a new greeting each day. The script is written fresh by an LLM each morning; a text-to-speech model turns it into audio that sound natural. The flow is deliberately straightforward. Chucka reads the vault, builds the dashboard and passes the dashboard data into a prompt. The script generator also receives Melbourne weather from wttr.in. The opencode CLI runs the LLM and writes the spoken summary. Audio is rendered, converted to Ogg/Opus with ffmpeg, then sent through a local OpenWA gateway to WhatsApp. A macOS launchd job starts the whole run at 7am. From start to send, a full run takes about two minutes. The voice part The first version had no voice at all. later, I added a spoken summary. The first voice came from macOS say . It did the job, though “morning radio” was perhaps a generous description of the sound. Then came the voice hunt. I set up local voice cloning with VoiceStudio , created voice profiles, auditioned three energy samples and picked a voice profile I named Pepper. I sped it up to about 1.08×, ran a full rehearsal and adjusted the prompt so the script could include inline emotion tags as well. Finding a voice with morning energy was the hardest part. Chucka uses a three-tier voice chain. The primary option is VoiceStudio / OmniVoice running locally on my Mac. If that app is unavailable, it falls back to Gemini TTS in the cloud. If that also fails, macOS say is the last resort. The final option is robotic, but dependable. The boring 80% is reliability Getting audio out of a model is only one part of sending a useful message every morning. The rest is making sure it arrives. Chucka sends through a local OpenWA gateway. I learned that a status of sent means the message has been queued, not necessarily delivered. After catching a silent drop, I changed the runner to wait for a delivered or read confirmation before shutting anything down. “Sent” and “delivered” are not synonyms when you’re relying on a message to start your day. From personal script to open source Open-sourcing it was also a forcing function. A script that only works on my machine can get away with mysterious assumptions. A repository for other people needs clearer setup steps and a cleaner boundary between the code and my own configuration. Making it public pushed me to tidy the edges. Chucka isn’t a product launch or a claim that I’ve solved personal productivity. It’s one person automating information that already exists, and adding a voice and a face to it. The source of truth remains Obsidian; the briefing is just a more convenient way to meet the day. For now, I’ll keep using Chucka daily and refining the voice and its energy. The point was never to build the biggest system. It was to make something small enough to finish, useful enough to keep, and tidy enough to share. Chucka is open source under the MIT licence: https://github.com/aminkh17/Chucka

title: How to validate an email list in Python without SMTP (syntax, MX, disposable)
author: PennyData
summary: Disclosure: I publish the Apify actor used below (pennydata/bulk-email-validator-no-smtp) and it was built with AI assistance (Claude). This is a how-to, not a benchmark. Short answer: this runs syntax, DNS/MX, disposable and role-address checks on a list of emails, without ever opening a connection to a mail server. from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( " YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN " ) run = client . actor ( " pennydata/bulk-email-validator-no-smtp " ). call ( run_input = { " emails " : [ " test@gmail.com " , " info@example.com " , " bob@mailinator.com " ]} ) rows = list ( client . dataset ( run [ " defaultDatasetId " ]). iterate_items ()) keep = [ r [ " email " ] for r in rows if r [ " valid " ] and not r [ " isRole " ]] Before a newsletter send you want to drop malformed addresses, dead domains and throwaway inboxes. Many validators do this by opening SMTP connections to the recipient's mail server, which is slow and can get your IP flagged. This actor never contacts a mail server: it checks syntax and DNS only. 1. Input { "emails" : [ "test@gmail.com" , "info@example.com" ] } You can also pass csvUrl (a public CSV; it uses the column whose header contains "email"), maxEmails and concurrency . Duplicates are validated once. (Full call shown at the top.) Actor page: https://apify.com/pennydata/bulk-email-validator-no-smtp 3. Output Real rows from running the validation code locally (MX lists shortened, checkedAt omitted): { "email" : "test@gmail.com" , "valid" : true , "status" : "deliverable_domain" , "reason" : null , "domain" : "gmail.com" , "hasMx" : true , "hasARecord" : true , "isDisposable" : false , "isRole" : false , "isFreeProvider" : true , "didYouMean" : null } { "email" : "info@example.com" , "valid" : false , "status" : "invalid_domain" , "reason" : "null_mx" , "domain" : "example.com" , "mxRecords" : [], "hasMx" : false , "hasARecord" : true , "isDisposable" : false , "isRole" : true , "isFreeProvider" : false , "didYouMean" : null } { "email" : "bob@mailinator.com" , "valid" : false , "status" : "disposable" , "reason" : "disposable_domain" , "domain" : "mailinator.com" , "hasMx" : true , "isDisposable" : true , "isRole" : false } Statuses: deliverable_domain , fallback_a_record , disposable , invalid_domain , invalid_syntax , unknown (DNS failed after retries). A SUMMARY record holds counts per status. isRole flags info@ , admin@ , noreply@ style addresses and didYouMean suggests fixes for typos of big providers. Honest limits It cannot tell whether a specific mailbox exists. valid: true means well-formed with a domain that accepts mail. Catch-all domains and non-existent users on real domains pass. Disposable detection uses the open disposable-email-domains list (CC0); brand-new throwaway services are missed until it updates. Role, free-provider and typo lists are short, hand-curated lists. DNS answers change over time, so rerun before a big send. Pricing is pay per event ($0.0008 per validated email at the time of writing; unknown rows are not charged). title: Round once, split later: 13 Python tests for LRC timestamps
author: Neuhaus Barsuhn
summary: Disclosure: this is a project-associated, AI-generated developer walkthrough prepared for the AI LRC Generator team. The standalone example and synthetic tests were executed locally; this is not a description of the product's internal implementation or a benchmark of audio recognition. A timestamp serializer looks like a small formatting task until a rounded value crosses a boundary. An input just below a minute can become exactly a minute at the precision chosen for export. If the code splits the original value into minutes and seconds before rounding, it can produce a seconds field that should have carried into the next minute. The useful design question is therefore not only how many decimal places to print. It is which units the function accepts, when rounding happens, and which invariants should hold after that decision. This example uses integer centiseconds as its output units and a deliberately narrow contract. One public function accepts nonnegative integer milliseconds. A second accepts unsigned ASCII decimal seconds as text and rounds directly to centiseconds. Both use round-half-up, then split the already rounded total into fields. They do not open recordings, infer words, repair cue order or validate an entire lyric document. Keeping that boundary explicit makes the small module easier to test and prevents its tests from being presented as evidence about problems the code does not attempt to solve. State the representation before writing the formatter The chosen output is a bracketed minute, seconds and hundredths representation. Minutes have a minimum width of two digits but are not wrapped at an hour. Seconds and hundredths always stay inside their respective ranges because they are obtained from integer division after rounding. This is an example policy, not a claim that every player accepts an arbitrarily wide minute field. A real export pipeline may need additional limits for its destination. Those limits should be a separate validation decision rather than an accidental side effect of using a clock or date formatting API. The millisecond interface intentionally rejects floats and booleans. In Python, booleans are integer subclasses, so a broad integer instance check can admit values that were probably not intended as durations. The exact type check here is a policy choice for a small teaching interface. A larger application could accept more numeric types, but it should document their conversion and error behavior. Silent truncation is particularly unhelpful when a caller believes it supplied a fractional duration. Rejecting the unsupported type makes that disagreement visible at the boundary instead of hiding it inside a plausible-looking timestamp. Round the total, then split the fields For integer milliseconds, adding five before integer division by ten implements the selected half-up rule for nonnegative values. The result is a total number of centiseconds. Dividing that total by six thousand produces minutes and a remainder; dividing the remainder by one hundred produces seconds and hundredths. A carry across a second or minute is already represented in the rounded total, so the formatting step does not need a collection of special-case repairs. The function is small because the arithmetic order does most of the work. The decimal-text interface should not round through an intermediate millisecond value. Consider the textual duration 59.9949 seconds. Rounding that first to milliseconds yields 59.995 seconds, which rounds again to 60.00 at centisecond precision. Rounding the original decimal directly to centiseconds yields 59.99. Neither intermediate operation is mysterious; the mismatch comes from composing two quantization steps. If the intended output precision is already known, perform that quantization once. If an upstream system has already delivered integer milliseconds, treat that as its explicit input representation rather than pretending the earlier precision is still available. """ Strict example LRC serialization; no audio processing or file I/O. """ from decimal import Decimal , ROUND_HALF_UP , localcontext import re _SECONDS = re . compile ( r " [0-9]+(?:\.[0-9]+)? " , re . ASCII ) def _stamp ( cs : int ) -> str : minutes , remainder = divmod ( cs , 6000 ) seconds , hundredths = divmod ( remainder , 100 ) return f " [ { minutes : 02 d } : { seconds : 02 d } . { hundredths : 02 d } ] " def from_milliseconds ( ms : int ) -> str : """ Nonnegative integer milliseconds, round half up to a centisecond. """ if type ( ms ) is not int : raise TypeError ( " milliseconds must be an int, not a bool or float " ) if ms < 0 : raise ValueError ( " milliseconds must be nonnegative " ) return _stamp (( ms + 5 ) // 10 ) def from_seconds_text ( text : str ) -> str : """ ASCII decimal seconds; round once, directly to centiseconds. """ if not isinstance ( text , str ): raise TypeError ( " seconds must be decimal text " ) if not 1 <= len ( text ) <= 80 or _SECONDS . fullmatch ( text ) is None : raise ValueError ( " expected 1-80 characters of unsigned decimal seconds " ) with localcontext () as context : context . prec = max ( 28 , len ( text ) + 4 ) cs = int (( Decimal ( text ) * 100 ). to_integral_value ( rounding = ROUND_HALF_UP )) return _stamp ( cs ) Keep decimal parsing separate from permissive conversion The accepted textual syntax is intentionally smaller than everything Decimal can parse. It permits ordinary unsigned decimal digits with an optional fractional part. It rejects whitespace, signs, exponent notation, missing digits around the decimal point and special values. That policy avoids accepting alternate representations merely because a conversion library happens to understand them. It also gives callers one clear normalization boundary. This is not an argument that other syntaxes are universally unsafe; an application can support them when it has a reason, but that decision should be deliberate and covered by tests. The eighty-character limit is an example bound for this interface, not an estimate of a reasonable recording duration. The local decimal context has enough precision for the accepted text before multiplication by one hundred. That matters because parsing a long decimal exactly does not guarantee that subsequent arithmetic will ignore the active context's precision. A long-input fixture checks that the intended carry is preserved. For a production service, resource limits, destination limits and how errors reach callers would still need their own review. The small bound and a passing fixture do not constitute a security audit. Test the boundaries that explain the design Save the module as lrc_clock.py and the following suite as test_lrc_clock.py in the same directory. Run python3 -m unittest -v from that directory. The suite was actually executed locally with Python's standard library: thirteen test methods passed, including subtests for several invalid inputs. The fixtures cover zero, rounding ties, second and minute carries, an hour boundary without clock wrapping, wide minutes, rejected types, strict decimal syntax and the double-rounding example. They are synthetic examples chosen to exercise this serializer's contract, not a sample of real recordings or a player compatibility study. import unittest from lrc_clock import from_milliseconds , from_seconds_text class ClockTests ( unittest . TestCase ): def test_zero ( self ): self . assertEqual ( from_milliseconds ( 0 ), " [00:00.00] " ) def test_integer_rounding_boundary ( self ): self . assertEqual ( from_milliseconds ( 4 ), " [00:00.00] " ) self . assertEqual ( from_milliseconds ( 5 ), " [00:00.01] " ) def test_second_carry ( self ): self . assertEqual ( from_milliseconds ( 994 ), " [00:00.99] " ) self . assertEqual ( from_milliseconds ( 995 ), " [00:01.00] " ) def test_minute_carry ( self ): self . assertEqual ( from_milliseconds ( 59994 ), " [00:59.99] " ) self . assertEqual ( from_milliseconds ( 59995 ), " [01:00.00] " ) def test_no_hour_wrap ( self ): self . assertEqual ( from_milliseconds ( 3599995 ), " [60:00.00] " ) def test_wide_minutes ( self ): self . assertEqual ( from_milliseconds ( 6000000 ), " [100:00.00] " ) def test_negative_integer ( self ): with self . assertRaises ( ValueError ): from_milliseconds ( - 1 ) def test_strict_integer_type ( self ): for value in ( True , False , 1.5 , " 10 " , None ): with self . subTest ( value = value ), self . assertRaises ( TypeError ): from_milliseconds ( value ) def test_decimal_without_double_rounding ( self ): self . assertEqual ( from_seconds_text ( " 59.9949 " ), " [00:59.99] " ) self . assertEqual ( from_seconds_text ( " 59.9950 " ), " [01:00.00] " ) def test_half_up_and_leading_zeroes ( self ): self . assertEqual ( from_seconds_text ( " 0.125 " ), " [00:00.13] " ) self . assertEqual ( from_seconds_text ( " 000.0099 " ), " [00:00.01] " ) self . assertEqual ( from_seconds_text ( " 12 " ), " [00:12.00] " ) def test_invalid_text ( self ): for value in ( "" , " " , " -1 " , " +1 " , " 1e2 " , " NaN " , " Infinity " , " .5 " , " 1. " , " 1:02 " , " ١ " , " 1 \n " , " 0 " * 81 ): with self . subTest ( value = value ), self . assertRaises ( ValueError ): from_seconds_text ( value ) def test_text_type ( self ): with self . assertRaises ( TypeError ): from_seconds_text ( 0.125 ) def test_long_input_keeps_precision ( self ): self . assertEqual ( from_seconds_text ( " 1 " * 40 + " .995 " ), from_milliseconds ( int ( " 1 " * 40 ) * 1000 + 995 )) if __name__ == " __main__ " : unittest . main () The expected strings are intentionally literal in the boundary tests. Computing an expected timestamp by calling the same formatting helper would make the tests less independent and could reproduce the same mistake on both sides of an assertion. The long-input test uses the separately defined integer-millisecond path as a cross-check, while the shorter decimal boundaries still have fixed expected strings. These approaches complement each other. None replaces a careful review of the contract, and a large number of assertions would not make an undocumented rounding rule correct for every consumer. Connect formatting tests to an honest export workflow A lyric editor can still need human review even when its serializer is well tested. Someone must check that the words and timing correspond to the exact recording and that the destination understands the chosen format. A browser workspace such as this lrc generator supports editable lyric text, line timestamps, offset adjustments, previews and lyric or subtitle exports. Editing and exports are free; automatic audio processing requires a verified account and credits. Consult its current pricing and storage terms. The module above is a standalone illustration, not a claim about how that service implements exports. Keep this serializer behind a clear application boundary. Resolve the intended timing representation before calling it, preserve the editable source and make validation errors useful to the caller. Do not infer an offset, delete a repeated line or repair a recording-version mismatch inside a formatting function. Those actions require context the function does not have. An export pipeline can coordinate several small components without making each component responsible for every problem. That separation also makes it easier to state which behavior a local test result does and does not support. Finally, test the actual exported file in the intended player or editor when that environment is available. Check characters, cue order and the features expected at the destination rather than treating a successful download as proof of compatibility. If destination testing is unavailable, report that limitation. The practical benefit of rounding once and testing boundaries is a more understandable piece of the pipeline, not a promise of perfect synchronized lyrics. Clear units, explicit conversion rules and narrowly stated evidence make the next review more useful than a timestamp that merely looks convincing.

title: How to Coordinate Multi-Agent AI Swarms Without Cloud Deadlocks: A Distributed Task Board MCP Server
author: johann
summary: How to Coordinate Multi-Agent AI Swarms Without Cloud Deadlocks: A Distributed Task Board MCP Server in Python In 2026, single-agent prompts are legacy. Developers and autonomous engineering teams run multi-agent swarms in parallel: one agent refactors legacy code, a second generates unit tests, a third updates architectural documentation, and a fourth audits security vulnerabilities. However, as soon as you spin up multiple LLM agents (Claude Desktop, Cursor, LangGraph, CrewAI) simultaneously on a project, you run into three critical failure modes: Race Conditions & Collision: Two agents pick up the same file or task at the exact same millisecond, overwriting each other's changes. Zombie Agent Lockup: An agent claiming a task hits an API rate limit or silent network timeout. The task remains locked indefinitely, freezing the entire downstream pipeline. Infrastructure Bloat: Setting up Redis, RabbitMQ, or Celery just so 3 local AI agents can talk to each other introduces massive maintenance overhead, port conflicts, and privacy risks. In this guide, we'll build AgentMesh , a lightweight, zero-dependency Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in Python that coordinates autonomous agent swarms with atomic mutual exclusion, DAG task dependencies, and automated zombie lease reclamation. The Architecture: Zero-Cloud Autonomous Coordination Instead of heavy message brokers, we leverage SQLite WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) with atomic BEGIN IMMEDIATE transactions. This provides microsecond-level ACID locking while allowing concurrent reads across dozens of parallel worker agents. +---------------------------------------------+ | Swarm Coordinator / User | +---------------------------------------------+ | (tools/create_task) v +---------------------------------------------+ | AgentMesh MCP Server | | (JSON-RPC stdio) | +---------------------------------------------+ / | \ +---------------+ +---------------+ +---------------+ | Agent Alpha | | Agent Beta | | Agent Gamma | | (Code Writer) | | (Test Runner) | | (Docs Builder)| +---------------+ +---------------+ +---------------+ \ | / v v v +---------------------------------------------------+ | SQLite WAL Concurrency Engine | |---------------------------------------------------| | 1. Atomic Mutual Exclusion Claiming | | 2. DAG Task Dependencies & Cycle Prevention | | 3. Heartbeat & Zombie Lease Reclamation | | 4. ACID Shared Memory Blackboard | +---------------------------------------------------+ 1. Atomic Mutual Exclusion: Preventing Agent Collisions Standard database updates are vulnerable to race conditions: -- DANGEROUS: Two agents can query and select task_101 simultaneously! SELECT id FROM tasks WHERE status = 'pending' LIMIT 1 ; UPDATE tasks SET status = 'in_progress' , claimed_by = 'agent-1' WHERE id = 'task_101' ; In AgentMesh, we wrap task claiming inside an isolated BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction. SQLite guarantees that only one agent acquires the exclusive reservation lock: def claim_task ( self , agent_id : str ) -> Optional [ Dict [ str , Any ]]: now = datetime . now ( timezone . utc ). isoformat () conn = self . _get_connection () try : conn . execute ( " BEGIN IMMEDIATE; " ) cursor = conn . execute ( """ SELECT id FROM tasks WHERE status = ' pending ' ORDER BY priority DESC, created_at ASC LIMIT 1; """ ) row = cursor . fetchone () if not row : conn . execute ( " COMMIT; " ) return None task_id = row [ " id " ] conn . execute ( """ UPDATE tasks SET status = ' in_progress ' , claimed_by = ?, claimed_at = ?, updated_at = ? WHERE id = ? AND status = ' pending ' ; """ , ( agent_id , now , now , task_id )) conn . execute ( " COMMIT; " ) return self . get_task ( task_id ) except Exception : conn . execute ( " ROLLBACK; " ) raise finally : conn . close () If 10 agents query claim_task concurrently, exactly 1 agent receives the task, while the remaining 9 proceed cleanly to the next available items without collisions. 2. DAG Dependency Resolution: Stopping Pipeline Collapses Real-world tasks are rarely flat. For example: Task A : Ingest database schema. Task B (depends on A): Generate migration scripts. Task C (depends on B): Run integration test harness. If an agent attempts Task B before Task A finishes, the pipeline crashes. AgentMesh introduces the depends_on parameter. When a task has unfulfilled dependencies, its status is held in blocked . When complete_task is called, the engine automatically evaluates the dependency graph and promotes unblocked tasks to pending : # Check dependent blocked tasks blocked_cursor = conn . execute ( " SELECT id, depends_on FROM tasks WHERE status = ' blocked ' ; " ) for b_row in blocked_cursor . fetchall (): b_id = b_row [ " id " ] deps = json . loads ( b_row [ " depends_on " ] or " [] " ) if deps : placeholders = " , " . join ( " ? " for _ in deps ) c_check = conn . execute ( f " SELECT COUNT(*) as cnt FROM tasks WHERE id IN ( { placeholders } ) AND status = ' completed ' ; " , deps ) if c_check . fetchone ()[ " cnt " ] == len ( deps ): # All parents finished successfully! Unblock task: conn . execute ( " UPDATE tasks SET status = ' pending ' , updated_at = ? WHERE id = ?; " , ( now , b_id )) 3. The Anti-Zombie Lease: Self-Healing Swarms What happens when an agent encounters an unhandled API exception, freezes, or dies mid-execution? Without leasing, that task remains stuck in in_progress forever. AgentMesh attaches a lease_timeout_sec (e.g., 60 seconds) to every claim. Active agents emit periodic heartbeat(task_id, agent_id) calls. If a worker disappears, the reclaim_zombies() monitor automatically resets the task: def reclaim_zombies ( self ) -> List [ Dict [ str , Any ]]: now = datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) reclaimed = [] with self . _get_connection () as conn : cursor = conn . execute ( " SELECT id, claimed_by, last_heartbeat, lease_timeout_sec FROM tasks WHERE status = ' in_progress ' ; " ) for row in cursor . fetchall (): last_hb = datetime . fromisoformat ( row [ " last_heartbeat " ]) lease_sec = row [ " lease_timeout_sec " ] or 60 if now - last_hb > timedelta ( seconds = lease_sec ): conn . execute ( """ UPDATE tasks SET status = ' pending ' , claimed_by = NULL, last_heartbeat = NULL WHERE id = ?; """ , ( row [ " id " ],)) reclaimed . append ({ " task_id " : row [ " id " ], " reclaimed_from " : row [ " claimed_by " ]}) return reclaimed 4. Connecting to Claude Desktop & Cursor Because AgentMesh communicates over the standardized Model Context Protocol (MCP) , connecting it to your favorite AI environment takes seconds. In your claude_desktop_config.json : { "mcpServers" : { "agentmesh" : { "command" : "python" , "args" : [ "-m" , "agentmesh.cli" , "run" ] } } } Now, Claude or Cursor can autonomously call: create_task(title="Refactor auth module", priority=5) claim_task(agent_id="claude-3-7-sonnet") complete_task(task_id="task_abc", agent_id="claude-3-7-sonnet", result={"diff": "+12 -4"}) Open Source vs. Enterprise Pro We have released the core AgentMesh Lite as free, open-source software: 📦 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/johannschiffer/agentmesh-mcp Features: SQLite WAL atomic task claiming, priority queue, board status reporting, and full MCP stdio protocol compliance. title: One Developer Rebuilt Adobe Creative Suite Using AI: Is This the Future of Software Development?
author: grandmaster
summary: By BET INFINITY 24×7 Editorial Team | October 21, 2026 The software industry is witnessing a fascinating shift. Tools that once required large engineering teams, years of development, and substantial financial investment are increasingly being challenged by smaller teams and independent developers using artificial intelligence. One of the most talked-about examples in October 2026 is ArtCraft , an ambitious collection of open-source alternatives to Adobe's professional creative applications. Software developer Brandon Thomas has attracted widespread attention for using Anthropic's Claude AI and the Rust programming language to build applications that attempt to reproduce familiar creative workflows. The project raises an important question: If one experienced developer can use AI to recreate parts of a major commercial software suite, what does that mean for the future of software development? What Happened? The AI-Powered Adobe Alternative In early October 2026, reports began circulating about ArtCraft, a project developing free alternatives to several popular Adobe applications. The growing collection includes: PhotoCraft: An alternative inspired by Adobe Photoshop. ImageCraft: A vector graphics application inspired by Illustrator. FilmCraft: A video editing alternative inspired by Premiere Pro. LightCraft: A photography workflow application inspired by Lightroom. MotionCraft: A motion graphics alternative inspired by After Effects. PdfCraft: A PDF editing tool inspired by Acrobat. LayoutCraft: A publishing and layout application inspired by InDesign. These are independently developed alternatives, not official Adobe products or copies of Adobe's proprietary source code. Thomas reportedly used Claude Opus 5.5 to assist with development, while Rust served as a major implementation language. The project's ambition is remarkable, but its applications remain works in progress. Independent reviews have identified missing features, bugs, and significant differences from mature commercial tools. Why This Development Matters For decades, sophisticated software development has required specialized expertise, extensive testing, and substantial resources. AI-assisted programming is beginning to change part of that equation. Modern coding assistants can help developers generate code, understand existing implementations, build interface components, write tests, and accelerate repetitive engineering tasks. This does not eliminate the need for experienced developers. Instead, it can allow them to focus more attention on architectural decisions, product functionality, security, and user experience. ArtCraft illustrates both the possibilities and limitations of this approach. A small development team may now be able to produce an impressive early prototype far more quickly than was previously practical. Transforming that prototype into secure, reliable, professional-grade software is another challenge entirely. Is AI Making Traditional Software Development Obsolete? Not necessarily. Generating application code is only one part of building successful software. Production systems still require: Reliable architecture and maintainable code Security reviews and vulnerability management Performance optimization Scalable infrastructure Reliable APIs and third-party integrations Testing, monitoring, and long-term maintenance A visually convincing application may still struggle with complicated file formats, large workloads, data integrity, and compatibility with existing workflows. The ArtCraft story demonstrates that AI can lower barriers to software creation without removing the importance of engineering quality. What This Means for Startups and Technology Businesses The implications extend beyond graphic design software. Startups developing financial technology, e-commerce systems, sports technology platforms, and enterprise applications can all benefit from more efficient development workflows. AI-assisted engineering can help teams experiment with new features, validate product ideas, and reduce time spent on repetitive programming tasks. For businesses building complex digital platforms, however, speed must be balanced with reliability. Consider a sports data platform processing frequent live updates. Generating the initial application interface may be relatively straightforward, but delivering accurate information consistently requires resilient API connections, efficient data processing, infrastructure monitoring, and careful system design. These engineering fundamentals remain essential regardless of how much code is generated by artificial intelligence. Technology companies such as BET INFINITY 24×7 operate in this broader software development ecosystem, with a focus on custom iGaming platforms, sports technology, API integration, and digital solutions for businesses. As AI development tools evolve, the combination of automated coding assistance and experienced engineering is likely to become increasingly valuable across specialized software markets. The Open-Source Opportunity Another interesting aspect of ArtCraft is its open-source approach. Open-source software allows developers to inspect, modify, and contribute to publicly available code under the applicable licence. This can encourage experimentation, peer review, and collaboration. However, open source does not automatically guarantee reliability or legal clearance. Developers adopting unfamiliar projects should examine licence terms, dependencies, security practices, and compatibility before using them in production. Software that closely imitates existing commercial applications may also raise intellectual property questions, even when its underlying code is independently written. The Future: Smaller Teams, Bigger Ambitions The most significant lesson from ArtCraft is not that established software companies will disappear. It is that the economics of developing software may be changing. AI can make early-stage development faster and lower the technical barriers for ambitious projects. Independent developers and smaller businesses may gain the ability to compete in markets that previously demanded much larger engineering budgets. But successful software companies will still need to provide dependable products, customer support, security, continuous improvements, and clear value to users. The next generation of software development will likely reward companies that combine AI-assisted productivity with thoughtful architecture and strong engineering practices. Conclusion The ArtCraft Adobe alternatives have sparked an important conversation about the future of commercial software. They demonstrate how experienced developers can use powerful AI coding tools to produce ambitious applications at extraordinary speed. They also remind us that creating a working prototype and delivering a mature, dependable product are fundamentally different achievements. AI is not simply changing how developers write code. It is changing what individuals, startups, and technology teams can attempt to build. And that may prove more significant than any single Adobe alternative. title: 🔓 IDOR / BOLA: How to Find the #1 API Vulnerability — and Actually Prove It
author: Krishna Kumar
summary: Broken Object Level Authorization — IDOR, to most of us — is the single most common serious bug in modern APIs. It sits at #1 on the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) , and it's the one I watch sail past a scanner, past a code review, and straight into production, where it lives for years. Not because it's clever. Because it's boring : the application carefully checks who you are , and then forgets to check whether the thing you just asked for is actually yours . This guide walks the whole path — what IDOR/BOLA is, how it works, how to find it, and the part most write-ups skip entirely: how to prove it , cleanly, without touching a single real user's data. What you'll learn By the end you'll be able to recognize where object-level authorization breaks, test an endpoint for it with two accounts you control, and — most importantly — turn "this looks vulnerable" into a report that triages instead of bouncing. Prerequisites Basic familiarity with HTTP requests, REST APIs, and how a bearer token or session cookie identifies you to a server. If you've ever opened your browser's dev tools and watched the Network tab, you're ready. What is IDOR / BOLA? Two names, one root cause. IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) is the classic bug-bounty name. An app exposes a reference to an internal object — /orders/1002 , ?user_id=55 , {"account":"ACME-9"} — and lets you tamper with it. BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization) is what OWASP calls the same thing on the API Security Top 10 , where it ranks first . The vulnerability is this: an endpoint accepts an identifier for some object and returns (or modifies) that object without checking whether the caller is allowed to touch it . The server confirmed you're logged in. It never confirmed the object is yours. How it works: the technical details Imagine an app that shows your invoice. With your valid bearer token, you request: GET /api/v1/invoices/1002 You're invoice 1002 . Out of curiosity, you change one digit: GET /api/v1/invoices/1003 If the server responds 200 OK with someone else's invoice (same valid token of yours), that's IDOR. Your token was valid, so you passed authentication . The server never asked the only question that mattered — "does this user own invoice 1003?" — so it failed authorization . That's the entire bug. Authentication asks who are you . Authorization asks are you allowed . IDOR is what happens when an app does the first and skips the second at the object level. Where IDOR hides It's rarely as obvious as a number in the URL. Look for object references in every part of the request: Sequential IDs — /users/55 , /orders/1002 . The easy case; just add or subtract. UUIDs and random IDs — /files/3fa85f64-5717-... . A non-guessable ID is not an authorization control. If that UUID ever leaks — in a response, a referrer header, a shared link, another endpoint's output — the object is still unprotected. The request body — {"account_id": 9} in a POST / PUT / PATCH . Headers and cookies — X-Account-Id , tenant headers. Nested and chained resources — /orgs/1/projects/44/secrets . The app checks your access to org 1 but not to project 44 . Non-GET methods — the juicy ones. A DELETE /comments/88 or PATCH /users/55/role that doesn't check ownership is a write-IDOR, often more severe than a read. Blind / stateful IDOR — nothing useful comes back in the response, but the action still happened (you changed another user's setting). You prove these by side effect, not by the response body. Detection is not proof Here's where most hunters stop too early — and where reports get closed as "informational." Detecting an IDOR is seeing that a different ID returns 200 instead of 403 . That's a signal. It is not a finding. Proving an IDOR is showing that the response contains data that belongs to a different account — and that you can reproduce it on demand. A 200 on its own could be an empty object, a decoy, a cached page, or your own data echoed back. The proof is the cross-account data , not the status code. Before you write a single word of a report, make the finding survive three questions: Can you reproduce it on demand? Twice, from a clean session. A one-off 200 is a coincidence, and it will come back "cannot reproduce." Can you show impact, not just presence? "The endpoint returned 200" is presence. "Account A read account B's email, phone, and address" is impact. Is it in scope, and is your proof safe? Demonstrate with accounts you own . Never pull a real customer's record to "prove" it — that turns a bounty into an incident. Reproduce, impact, scope. A finding that answers all three is real. How to find it (and prove it safely) The clean method needs two accounts you control — call them Alice and Bob. Both are yours, so any data you touch is your own test data. That single habit is what makes your proof both convincing and in-scope. Log in as Bob . Create or open an object — an invoice, a profile, a note. Record its ID ( BOB_ID ) and one unique field you'll recognize later (say, bob+test@you.example ). Log in as Alice and grab her token. As Alice , request Bob's object. Both accounts are yours, so $TOKEN_A is Alice's and the object belongs to Bob (also you): curl -s https://api.target.example/api/v1/users/BOB_ID/profile -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN_A" A vulnerable server responds 200 OK with Bob's record: { "id": "BOB_ID", "email": "bob+test@you.example", "phone": "+1-555-0137" } Alice's token just read Bob's profile. That response — Bob's unique email, returned under Alice's token — is the proof. Not that the endpoint "looks" authorizable. That it handed over another account's data, on demand. Show the control for contrast, so there's no ambiguity — the same request with Bob's own token: curl -s https://api.target.example/api/v1/users/BOB_ID/profile -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN_B" That returns 200 OK too — but it's Bob reading Bob, exactly what should happen. The gap between those two requests is the entire finding. For a write-IDOR , prove it with a harmless, reversible change on your own second account — flip a display name on Bob's object using Alice's token, screenshot it, flip it back. You've demonstrated control without destroying anything. If you're testing at scale, Burp Suite's Autorize or AuthMatrix extensions automate exactly this: they replay every request with a second account's session and flag the responses that shouldn't have succeeded. But the logic is the same two-account swap you can do with curl . Write the report as proof, not a label The report that gets paid is an equation, not a noun. Don't send "IDOR in profile endpoint." Send: the exact request (method, path, which token), the response, with the unique cross-account field highlighted, the control request for contrast, one line of impact: "Any authenticated user can read any other user's PII by changing the user ID — no further privileges required." Same bug, two reports. One says IDOR in /users . The other shows Alice's token returning Bob's email, with the baseline next to it. The first gets closed. The second gets a bounty. The difference was never the bug — it was the proof. How developers prevent it Enforce object-level authorization on every object access. For every request that names an object, ask server-side: does this subject own, or have an explicit grant to, this specific object? Not "is this user logged in." Not "is this user an admin." Centralize the check. Per-endpoint, hand-rolled ownership checks drift and get forgotten on the next new route. A single, mandatory authorization layer is far harder to bypass. Don't lean on unguessable IDs. UUIDs raise the cost of discovery ; they are not authorization . Treat them as usernames, not passwords. Test across roles and tenants. Most BOLA ships because QA only ever tested with one account. Test cross-user and cross-tenant on purpose. Common mistakes to avoid Hunters: testing with a single account. If you only have one identity, you will never see IDOR — you need a second object you're not supposed to reach. And don't assume a UUID endpoint is safe; check whether that ID leaks anywhere else first. Developers: confirming authentication and calling it a day; scattering ownership checks across controllers so one new endpoint quietly ships without one. Automating the proof step The two-account swap is mechanical, which means it's automatable — and that's exactly the problem my team works on with Xalgorix , an open-source AI pentester. Its methodology has a dedicated phase for object-level authorization that tests access across roles and tenants , and — true to the theme of this post — every finding is replayed with a proof payload and then re-verified by a separate pass before it ever reaches the report, non-destructively. You can self-host it (Apache-2.0) or run it on Xalgorix Cloud . Disclosure: I work on Xalgorix. The two-account method above stands entirely on its own, with or without any tool. Try it yourself Practice only on targets you own or are explicitly authorized to test. These are built for it: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — the free "Access control vulnerabilities" labs are the best structured introduction to IDOR anywhere. OWASP crAPI ("Completely Ridiculous API") — a deliberately vulnerable API with real BOLA to find. VAmPI — a small vulnerable REST API, great for practicing the two-account swap with curl . Spin one up, create two accounts, and go read the account that isn't yours — then write the finding the way we did above. Conclusion IDOR/BOLA tops the API Top 10 not because it's hard to exploit, but because it's easy to miss: the app does the visible half of security — logging you in — and skips the quiet half — checking that the object is yours. Find it with two accounts. Prove it with cross-account data, not a status code. Report it as an equation, not a label. Do that, and you stop sending findings that come back "informational" — and start sending the ones programs remember. 🔐 If this was useful, follow me for more hands-on web & API security write-ups. 🔗 Connect with me on LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/xalgord/

title: We gave our MCP server an undo button
author: Quentin Wendegass
summary: Letting an AI agent change your product's settings is only reasonable if you can take it all back. So every change our MCP server makes goes into a run that can be undone in one step. This is how it works, and the decisions that turned out to be hard. In July 2025, Replit's AI agent deleted a company's production database during a code freeze, then told the user the data couldn't be recovered. It could. Replit had a rollback, and the user restored everything from a checkpoint. The agent just didn't know the feature existed . Two lessons from that story shaped what we built: the agent has to know that undo exists, and people have to be able to undo without asking the agent. We build Privatrak , a cookieless analytics tool. Its MCP server lets Claude, Cursor or Codex do more than read your analytics. They can set them up: feature rules that name what people click, funnels, dashboards, and marking click problems as fixed. 17 of its 44 tools change something. Most MCP servers with write access rely on the client asking before each call. We wanted one more thing: after an agent has made twenty changes, you see all of them in one list and undo them in one step, without losing what you or a colleague changed in between. Asking first isn't enough Claude asks before it runs a tool marked destructive. That's good, and we set our tool annotations carefully for it. But it depends on the server labelling its tools honestly, which is why the MCP specification tells clients to treat those labels as untrusted unless the server is trusted. And it protects one call at a time, while an agent's work isn't one call. Setting up a project takes a dozen or twenty writes: rules, a funnel built on those rules, a dashboard whose widgets query them. Nobody reads the fifteenth confirmation as carefully as the first. Security people call this confirmation fatigue, and OWASP's list of risks for AI agents includes it. And the mistakes in a setup rarely show in a single call. They show later, when a dashboard counts the wrong thing. What you need then isn't another confirmation. You need to see everything the agent did as one unit, and to take that unit back. Developers have that for code in version control. Product settings usually have nothing like it. Undo has to live in the server Coding agents already have undo. Claude Code and Cursor keep checkpoints you can go back to. But both only cover files the agent edited. Claude Code's docs say changes made through commands aren't tracked, and Cursor's say restoring a checkpoint doesn't undo a database migration the agent ran. Once an agent calls an API, the client can't take it back. Only the service behind the API can. MCP doesn't help here either. The specification asks clients to keep a person in the loop and to confirm tool calls, but it has nothing for transactions or rollback. So if you want undo for what an agent does in your product, you build it into your MCP server. That's what the rest of this article is about. One task, one run The unit of undo is a setup run . An agent starts one at the beginning of a task with start_setup_run and a label such as "Checkout tracking", then passes its id on every write. The run answers the question "what did the assistant do?" Two rules make it reliable: Nothing happens outside a run. A write tool called without a run id starts a run itself and returns its id. Even an agent that ignores the instructions leaves a trail that can be undone. Runs that changed nothing don't clutter the list. If the API rejects a write, the tool deletes the run it had just started for it. In the API, a write joins a run through a header, X-Setup-Run-ID , not a body field. DELETE has no body, and all fourteen write operations should join the same way. A write without the header takes exactly the code path it always took, so adding runs changed nothing that already worked. The runs also show up in the dashboard under Settings, as AI assistant changes . The person who connected the assistant doesn't need the assistant to undo what it did. Record before and after, in the same transaction Every write that belongs to a run is saved together with a record of what it changed: the state before and the state after. Both are saved in one database transaction, so either both happen or neither does. The run is locked meanwhile, so nobody can undo it halfway through a write. The recorded state is the whole definition: a rule's name and conditions, a funnel's steps, a dashboard with its widgets. Everything undo needs to rebuild it. The database enforces the shape: a creation has no "before", a deletion has no "after". One detail cost us more time than the rest. Undo later compares these records with what is in the database now. If the same thing can be saved in two ways that mean the same, the comparison fails, and every undo looks like a conflict. So every write saves its input in exactly one form. Undo walks backwards Undo replays the run's changes newest first, in one transaction: Created becomes deleted. Updated gets back the fields the run changed. Deleted is recreated, with its original id. Newest first matters. An agent that created a rule and then renamed it has to unwind the rename before the creation. And if the run created something and later deleted it itself, there is nothing to do for it at all. The original id matters more than it sounds. Dashboards, funnels and links refer to things by id. A recreated rule even gets its original creation time back, because the order of rules decides which name the journey view shows for a click. Undo should leave the project reading exactly as before, not just something equivalent. Afterwards the run is marked as undone and its report is stored. Asking again returns the same report, and a write that tries to join an undone run is refused. The undo starts with the agent's last change and works back to its first. The funnel you renamed stays, and everything else goes. Never overwrite someone else's work This was the hardest decision. Between the agent's run and the undo, people keep working. Someone renames a widget the agent made, or fixes a rule's condition. Undo must not destroy that. So every change is checked before it is reverted: Undoing a creation requires the thing to still be exactly what the run created. Undoing an update requires every field the run changed to still hold the run's value. Fields the run didn't touch may have changed since. They are none of its business. A dashboard the run created that now holds someone else's widgets is not deleted. Recreating something that would go over the plan's limits is skipped, not forced through. When a check fails, that one change is skipped and reported with the reason, and the rest of the run is still undone. We considered stopping the whole undo instead. But then one widget someone renamed would keep an agent's entire setup in place. Skipping and reporting gives people the undo they asked for, minus exactly the things they have since made their own. What counts as someone's work was a decision too. Moving or resizing a widget doesn't count. Someone who drags an agent's widget aside hasn't made it theirs, and deleting it destroys nothing they did. The preview is the real undo, rolled back You want to see an undo before it happens. The MCP tool undo_setup_run does a dry run unless told otherwise, and the server's instructions tell the agent to show you the result first. In the dashboard, the dialog says "This is what undoing will do. Nothing has been changed yet." before the button. The preview isn't a separate prediction. It runs the actual undo, every check and every write, inside the transaction, and then rolls the transaction back. A prediction written as separate code drifts away from what undo really does, and then the preview is wrong exactly when it matters. One code path can't disagree with itself. Say what can't come back Some things can't be undone exactly, and pretending otherwise is worse than saying so. In Privatrak, a funnel counts from the day it is created. The per-visitor data that could recount earlier days is deleted every night, for privacy. That has two consequences for undo: Undoing a funnel the agent created also deletes the days it has counted since. The preview says how many. A funnel the agent deleted comes back with its name and steps, but it counts again from the undo. Its old days are gone, and the report says so. The rule we took from this: when undo can't be exact, the preview has to say what will be lost, before anyone confirms. Undo is the last line, not the only one Undo is what makes write access reasonable, but it sits behind other guards: Tools go through our own API. Each tool sends an ordinary request to our existing API, with the same authentication, validation, plan limits and project scoping as any other client. There is no second path to the data, so there is no second set of rules to get wrong. Write access is a fixed list. A read-only connection can reach a fixed list of API endpoints. Write access adds exactly the endpoints the write tools need, and nothing else. Tests fail if the tools and the lists disagree, in either direction. People choose at sign-in. Which projects the connection may see, and whether it may only read or also make changes. Every call names its project. The server keeps no "current project" that one chat could switch for another. The hints are honest. Creating isn't destructive. Updating, deleting and undoing are, so Claude asks before them. When we submitted Privatrak to Claude's connector directory , the undo made one more thing possible: a test plan that calls all 44 tools on a shared review account and ends by undoing everything it changed. If you build this yourself Pick the unit: one task, one run. Make every write join a run, even when the agent forgets to start one. Record the whole state before and after, in the same transaction as the write, saved in one fixed form so you can compare it later. Undo newest first, in one transaction, and recreate deleted things with their original ids. Check every change for conflicts. Skip and report; never force, and never give up on the whole run. Make the preview the real undo, rolled back. Say what can't come back, before it is lost. Put undo where people are: in the tool for the agent, and in your product's UI for everyone else. Privatrak's MCP server works with Claude, Cursor and Codex. Our docs show how to connect it.

title: Critical PHP warning: Security updates coming soon
author: Hacks.gr
summary: PHP maintainers have announced upcoming security updates for two high-severity vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both rated 9.2 in severity. Research suggests these flaws may impact PHP versions dating back to 2004. Reports have identified a tool, 'PHP2Shell,' purportedly capable of executing code on widely used platforms including Laravel, Drupal, and Joomla. Developers and sysadmins should prepare for an immediate update rollout. Because PHP is used to power a huge number of websites and applications on the internet, the development team asks administrators to prepare to immediately install updates as soon as they become available. Why is there concern? The warning came after reports emerged of a tool called “PHP2Shell.” According to this information, the tool appears to be able to allow third parties to take control of systems running popular platforms, including WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, Magento, Laravel, MediaWiki, phpBB, Symphony, and WHMCS. Although the exact details of how the tool works have not been fully confirmed, cybersecurity firm watchTowr has confirmed that the security vulnerabilities it relies on exist.
